body_markdown:
Research involving nearly 300 people with Parkinson’s disease found that higher levels of physical activity were associated with slower declines in thinking, memory, and movement over time.


Physical activity may play an important role in helping people with Parkinson’s disease maintain their cognitive abilities and physical function, according to a new study published in the medical journal *Neurology* on October 8, 2026.


The research suggests that people who remain more physically active may experience slower declines in thinking, memory, and movement compared with those who engage in less physical activity. The findings also highlight the potential importance of maintaining an active lifestyle over an extended period.


Although the results offer encouraging insights into Parkinson’s disease management, researchers caution that the study does not prove that exercise directly slows the progression of the condition. Further research is needed to understand the relationship between physical activity and changes in symptoms.


## Study Examines Physical Activity and Parkinson’s Disease


The study used data from the Cincinnati Cohort Biomarker Program and included nearly 300 people living with mild to moderate Parkinson’s disease.


Participants had an average age of 66, and approximately 33 percent were women. Researchers followed participants for up to seven years to examine how their reported physical activity levels related to changes in their cognitive abilities and motor function.


During the study, participants reported how much physical activity they typically completed each week. Their activities included moderate exercise, such as brisk walking and light swimming, as well as more vigorous activities, including jogging and fast cycling.


Researchers divided participants into three groups based on their reported weekly activity levels.


The least active group completed up to four hours of physical activity each week. The middle group reported between four and eight hours, while the most active group engaged in more than eight hours of activity weekly.


Participants also underwent annual assessments designed to measure their thinking, memory, and movement abilities.


The results showed that people reporting higher levels of physical activity experienced slower declines in cognitive performance and less worsening of motor symptoms over time.


These associations remained after researchers accounted for factors including age, sex, and the length of time participants had been living with Parkinson’s disease.


## Why Physical Activity May Matter


Parkinson’s disease is a progressive neurological condition that affects movement and can also influence thinking, memory, mood, and other aspects of daily life.


Common symptoms include tremors, muscle stiffness, slowed movement, and difficulties with balance and coordination. Symptoms can develop gradually, and their severity varies from person to person.


As the condition progresses, everyday activities such as walking, dressing, preparing meals, and maintaining balance may become increasingly challenging.


Physical activity can be an important part of managing these difficulties. Depending on an individual’s abilities and needs, exercise may help support strength, flexibility, balance, endurance, and mobility.


Activities such as walking, swimming, stationary cycling, and supervised strength training can provide opportunities to maintain physical function. Balance exercises and appropriately adapted movement programs may also help people work on coordination and stability.


The latest findings add to the growing interest in understanding how sustained physical activity relates to the long-term experience of Parkinson’s disease.


However, the study does not establish a specific biological mechanism explaining why more active participants experienced slower declines. Researchers will need additional evidence to determine whether exercise itself contributes to these differences and which types of activity may offer the greatest benefits.


## Consistency Over Time Could Be Important


Dong-Woo Ryu, MD, PhD, of the University of Cincinnati in Ohio, was the study’s author.


In a press release from the American Academy of Neurology, Ryu emphasized that the potential benefits of physical activity may depend not only on how much people exercise but also on how consistently they remain active over time.


This observation raises an important consideration for people living with Parkinson’s disease: maintaining a realistic, sustainable exercise routine may be more practical than attempting to complete demanding workouts that are difficult to continue.


For some people, this could mean taking regular walks, participating in a movement class, swimming at a comfortable pace, or following an exercise plan developed with a qualified professional.


The most appropriate activities will depend on an individual’s symptoms, fitness level, balance, medical history, and personal preferences.


People experiencing freezing episodes, frequent falls, significant dizziness, or other mobility challenges may need supervision or specialized exercise programs to reduce the risk of injury.


Ryu also cautioned that the differences observed between activity groups were relatively small, even though they could become more meaningful over time.


The researchers noted another limitation: participants generally demonstrated good thinking and memory abilities at the beginning of the study. Consequently, the results should be interpreted cautiously and cannot necessarily be applied to everyone living with Parkinson’s disease.


## Understanding the Limitations of the Research


One of the most important points is that the study identified an association rather than proving cause and effect.


People who are more physically active may differ from less active individuals in other ways. For example, they may have fewer mobility limitations, better overall health, or other characteristics that influence how their symptoms change.


It is also possible that people whose Parkinson’s symptoms progress more slowly are better able to remain physically active. This means the relationship could work in both directions.


Additionally, participants reported their own activity levels, which may not always reflect their actual exercise habits precisely.


The research also focused on people with mild to moderate Parkinson’s disease. Its findings may not apply equally to individuals with more advanced symptoms or substantial cognitive impairment.


Further studies, including research that follows participants over longer periods and examines different exercise programs, could help clarify these questions.


## Parkinson’s Disease: Current Treatment Options


According to the Parkinson’s Foundation, Parkinson’s disease affects millions of people worldwide and is associated with the gradual loss of nerve cells involved in producing dopamine, a chemical messenger that helps regulate movement.


There is currently no known cure for the condition. Nevertheless, treatments can help many people manage symptoms and maintain quality of life.


Treatment may include medication, physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and other supportive approaches. Some individuals may also be candidates for advanced treatments, depending on their symptoms and medical circumstances.


Exercise is not a replacement for prescribed medication or professional medical care. Instead, it may complement an individualized treatment plan.


Anyone considering a new exercise routine should consult a healthcare professional, particularly if Parkinson’s symptoms affect balance, coordination, blood pressure, or the ability to move safely.


## Conclusion


The new research provides further evidence of a potential relationship between physical activity and slower declines in cognitive and motor function among people with Parkinson’s disease.


Although the findings do not prove that exercise slows the underlying progression of the condition, they reinforce the importance of investigating physical activity as part of long-term Parkinson’s disease management.


For people living with the condition, regular movement may offer practical benefits when it is adapted to their abilities and incorporated into a broader care plan.


Future research will be essential to determine which activities are most effective, how much exercise may be beneficial, and whether maintaining consistent physical activity can directly influence disease progression.


Until then, the findings offer a reason to continue exploring safe, personalized approaches to staying active while recognizing that Parkinson’s disease affects each person differently.

1. *Neurology* , “Physical Activity and Progression of Parkinson Disease,” published October 8, 2026.
2. American Academy of Neurology, study press release.

The study describes associations between physical activity and changes in Parkinson’s disease symptoms; it does not establish that exercise causes slower disease progression. Consult a qualified healthcare professional before making changes to an exercise routine or treatment plan.
